schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make 'and now' the hinge, turning the history into obligation, and map the whole discourse from it; Ellicott sets the chapter beside Joshua's farewell and notes that life is put before possession.
Gill lists the mercies the 'therefore' looks back on; Calvin makes teachableness the beginning of an upright life, since one must first know what pleases God.
Henry says the sermon is too entire to divide, calls it the use and application of the foregoing history, and reads the demand for attention as binding on every later reading of the law.
Wesley divides statutes from judgments as duties to God and duties to men, so that the two comprehend both tables.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that additions weaken the law as surely as omissions, as Pharisaism proved, and trace the precept to Revelation 22 and to Christ's word about fulfilling the law; Ellicott notes the Hebrew says 'the word,' not 'the words'.
Gill allows both a textual and a practical reading; Calvin says none are true disciples of the law but those who take their wisdom from it alone.
Henry reports the same double reading, insists nothing can be added to God's perfect work without making it worse, and credits Jewish scrupulosity for the integrity of the Hebrew text.
Clarke turns the prohibition on the commentator: add no word God has not spoken, and give no comment tending to corrupt or weaken the revelation.

debates.question: Does the prohibition concern the text of the law or the practice of it?

sides.position: practice — neither commit what is forbidden nor omit what is commanded
doctrine and rite — add no invention, set aside nothing as superfluous
the substance rather than the wording, since the Hebrew reads 'the word'

3.pericope_label: Baal-peor: the dead and the survivors as evidence

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the pair a demonstration that keeping the law gives life, glossing 'clave' as clinging fast; Ellicott renders it 'your eyes are they that see' and puts the 24,000 dead in the younger generation, Moses' own hearers.

Gill traces the apostasy to the counsel of Balaam and the daughters of Moab and Midian; Calvin says the vengeance was too conspicuous to be hidden from the most ignorant, and limits the praise of their constancy to that one occasion.

5.pericope_label: The statutes faithfully taught, and Israel's wisdom in the sight of the nations

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch say history confirmed the claim, from the queen of Sheba to the heathen who sought God in Israel's law as their own religions dissolved; Ellicott notes that much of the law cannot be kept except by a chosen people in a protected land.

Gill has Moses delivering the law without adding or diminishing; Calvin answers the objection that the heathen despised it — no nation come to a right understanding would dare compare itself with Israel, and we are truly wise only when we depend on God's words.

Clarke says no worship then on earth was not wicked or ridiculous except this one, and points to the nations' borrowing of the Mosaic civil code; Wesley adds that the wisest heathen approved and translated these laws.

themes: the law's reputation among the nations

7.pericope_label: Two questions: a God so nigh, and statutes so righteous

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch locate Israel's attractive force in a God at hand when called on and a law the heathen never had, and add that where the knowledge of God is obscured, law and right are shaken with it; Ellicott finds the law distinctly in advance of its age.

Gill clears away number, territory and wealth as grounds of greatness, leaving the constitution in church and state; Calvin sets out the two reasons — God ready to help when called on, and instruction in perfect righteousness — and denies the Gentiles ever had such aid from deaf idols.

Wesley opens out God's nearness into miracles, presence, grace and answered prayer, and draws the political moral that a nation's greatness lies in the righteousness of its laws, not in pomp or empire.

themes: a God near to those who call

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss 'keep thy soul' as guarding life itself, and make the remembered facts the foundation of the true religion and the guarantee that distinguishes it from heathen religions whose founders offered no such proof; Ellicott observes that Israel plainly failed the command to teach, since a generation soon rose that knew not Jehovah.
Calvin reads the opening particle as 'this one thing remains,' and says extreme vigilance is needed because nothing is easier than for zeal to be suddenly forgotten or gradually to grow cold.

Clarke turns each clause on the soul's estate — divine things must be laid up in the heart, not only the memory — and argues from the very existence of the exhortation that men may finally fall from grace.

debates.question: Why is such an exhortation given at all?

sides.position: because those who let grace depart lose it, and may fall and rise no more
because the slothfulness of the flesh needs spurring and our unsteadfastness fortifying

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch pick out the twofold purpose of the assembly — that they might fear God lifelong and teach their children; Ellicott dates the Church of Israel from Sinai as the Church of Christ from Pentecost, and notes that the Greek for 'gather the people' is the verb behind ekklesia, the source of Stephen's 'church in the wilderness'.

Gill says the day was to be remembered above all others for its fire, smoke and trumpet; Calvin has Moses summon the people as eyewitnesses, and proves God the author of the doctrine from its object — that God be purely served.
Wesley meets the difficulty of the hearers' age: some stood there in their own persons, though young, and the rest in the loins of their parents.

themes: fear taught to be handed on

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'burning unto the midst of heaven' as a rhetorical description of the majesty of the pillar of fire, and state the consequence — Israel could see no form of God, only hear the voice of his words; Ellicott points to the blackness, darkness and tempest of Hebrews 12.

Gill places the people at the foot of the mountain, in its lower part; Calvin makes the burning mountain a proof that Moses was only God's minister, and prefers to read 'no similitude' not as a concession but as evidence that the voice was God's, since no man could have spoken unseen.

Gill sets the scene in cloud, fire and thick darkness; Calvin takes the verse for a confirmation of the second commandment, raises the objection that God appeared visibly to the patriarchs and prophets, and answers that such forms were a peculiar circumstance and a temporary sign, not a rule.
Henry explains why a voice and not a shape — faith comes by hearing, and to see God as he is not would do us hurt — and warns against idols in the heart where there are none in the sanctuary.
Wesley defines what was missing: no resemblance whereby God's essence, properties or actions were represented, such as the heathen used.

debates.question: If God appeared visibly to the patriarchs and prophets, why is a visible image forbidden?

sides.position: those appearances were a peculiar circumstance and a temporary sign, given to raise the mind above earthly elements
the objection stands as stated, since visible forms often testified his presence

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the order exact — no form seen, only a voice heard, and then the ten words written by God on two tables of stone.
Gill explains why the law is called a covenant: it carried God's requirements with promises annexed, and Israel's agreement to hear and obey.

themes: a text rather than a likeness

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch put the two commissions in sequence: the ten words came from God to the nation, and only then was Moses directed to teach the statutes of the Sinaitic legislation for Canaan.
Henry shows the threefold division at work — governed by the moral precepts, devotion by the ritual, justice by the judicial law — and adds that hearing is in order to doing.
Gill dates the second commission to the summons up the mount after the ten commandments were delivered.
Wesley labels the statutes and judgments here as the ceremonial and judicial laws, distinguished from the moral law.

themes: taught in the desert, kept in the land
the charge repeated under many verbs

15.pericope_label: Take good heed: no similitude seen, therefore no image made

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch draw the inference from the absence of any shape at Horeb, and take the following phrases as apposition explaining the prohibition rather than extending it; Ellicott registers how hard invisible worship was when every nation had its symbol, and recalls that Christians were once called atheists for having no visible God.

Clarke grounds the ban in God's nature as Spirit and argues that outward things diffuse the mind on sensible objects and prevent spiritual worship; Wesley notes that God, who elsewhere appeared in the fashion of a man, purposely avoided all such representation at this most solemn appearance.
Henry reads 'corrupt' as debauch: those who make images of God form notions of him that are an inlet to all impieties, and it is a spiritual adultery.
Gill observes that idolatry corrupts not only the worshippers but the word and worship of God.

debates.question: How does making an image 'corrupt' the maker?

sides.position: it debauches the mind by forming false notions of God; it is spiritual adultery
it exchanges the incorruptible God's glory for a creature, and degrades a man who was made to rule what he now worships
it draws the mind out to sensible objects and so prevents spiritual worship

17.pericope_label: The catalogue of forms: beast, fowl, creeping thing and fish

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the ban on animal images as a caution against imitating the animal worship of Egypt, and Ellicott allows the same allusion.

Henry gathers the whole catalogue into one argument, that the heathen worshipped by images of all these kinds because they would not admit the prophet's demonstration that the workman made it, therefore it is not God.
Gill instances the ox of the Egyptians, the sheep of the Thebans and the goat of the Mendesians, and traces serpent-worship back to the serpent that deceived our first parents.
Clarke fills out the Egyptian pantheon at close range — Apis the white bull, the ibis and hawk, serpents and the crocodile, and then monkeys, cats, the scarab, leeks and onions.

themes: the ranks of creation as idols

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch deny that God gave the heathen the heavenly bodies for service and hold that he allotted them for worship; Ellicott says the stars could protect no one nation, whereas Jehovah was pledged to Israel.

Gill grants that looking at the stars may be commendable and only warns that it is ensnaring if unguarded; Calvin exposes the subtler snare of imagining the stars to be somehow of God, and reads 'divided' as subjection — the sun our minister, the moon and stars our handmaid.

Clarke calls star-worship the oldest idolatry, credits astronomy with destroying it, and is severe on the astrologers who revive it; Wesley says these are creatures made not for the worship but for the use of men.
Henry notices the verb 'driven' — the heart walking after the eye — yet judges the temptation weak to anyone who reasons, since the Hebrew name of the sun means a servant.

debates.question: What does it mean that God 'divided' the host of heaven to all nations?

sides.position: he gave them to serve the nations with their light
holders: Onkelos, the Rabbins and Jerome (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: he permitted the nations to choose them as objects of worship
the word marks their subjection to men and the variety of their offices

themes: what the eye draws the heart to

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the verb the point — the nations were allotted the heavenly bodies, but Israel was taken, drawn out and separated to be a people of inheritance — and conclude that God must therefore be worshipped without image or form.
Gill reads the iron furnace as the figure of a refiner's fire, Egypt so called for the cruelty and bondage, and God's people brought out of the furnace of affliction purged of their dross.
Clarke takes the phrase literally and infers that the Israelites were employed in Egypt at the most laborious works of metallurgy, oppressive labour in so hot a climate.

debates.question: Is the 'iron furnace' a figure or a memory of Egyptian labour?

sides.position: a figure for the cruelty and refining of the bondage
a literal indication that Israel worked in metallurgy

21.pericope_label: Moses excluded from the land, and the warning renewed

schools.summary: Gill notes that Moses died in a mountain of Moab and was buried in a valley there; Calvin insists the mention is not expostulation but a magnifying of God's mercy — the pardon extended to them was denied to Moses — and adds that 'for your sakes' may as well be 'for your words'.
Keil and Delitzsch trace how the mention of Canaan leads Moses back to his own exclusion, and defend the oath reported here against Knobel's objection that no such oath appears in Numbers.
Clarke turns the fact into an argument: if God was angry with Moses so as to debar him, can those guilty of greater provocations think to escape?

debates.question: Is the oath Moses reports credible, since Numbers does not record it?

sides.position: no — the silence tells against it
holders: Knobel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: yes — the historical account plainly does not give every detail

themes: the fathers' sin and the children's

schools.summary: Gill explains the repetition by Moses' nearing death; Calvin removes the apparent inconsistency between forbidding images and forbidding their worship, restates that whatever confines our senses to earth is contrary to the covenant, reads the closing clause as a comparison, and answers the plea that images instruct the people.
Henry makes forgetting, not idolatry, the thing warned against — it is at the bottom of all our departures from God — and calls care and holy watchfulness the best helps against a bad memory.

debates.question: May images be retained as useful for the people's instruction?

sides.position: no — our wisdom is to acquiesce in what God has decreed, without disputing whether the thing forbidden is lawful
yes — they instruct the unlearned

schools.summary: Clarke sets the phrase against two things Israel had seen — an unconsuming fire on the mount and a consuming fire in the case of Korah; Wesley expands both names, a just and terrible God who will bear no rival or partner.
Ellicott follows the phrase into Hebrews 12, where it enforces the lessons not of Sinai but of the voice that speaks from heaven.

Henry divides the two names by what each implies — a jealous eye to discern an affront, a heavy hand to punish it — and then turns the argument round to ask why we should forsake a merciful God who will never forsake us.
Gill applies the consuming fire to God's enemies, and to idolaters above all, whose sin strikes at his being and glory.

themes: held by the bonds of love

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set out the supposed case and say growing old in the land means forgetfulness of past grace, not necessarily luxury; Ellicott finds the peril in the verb, which is literally 'shall slumber' — prosperity sends true religion to sleep and puts fashionable religion in its place.

Gill measures the clause as generations passed; Calvin explains that the warning runs to descendants because long possession hardens men in security, and it was as easy for God to drive out a settled posterity as to prevent their entering.

Gill treats the appeal as a matter of publicity; Calvin rejects the reading that makes heaven and earth a figure for angels and men, letting the personification stand, and compares the same figure in Moses' song and in Isaiah's indictment.

Keil and Delitzsch say heaven and earth are personified rather than standing for their inhabitants, and define the office exactly — they testify that God had warned the people, not that Israel was guilty.
Clarke identifies the form as a solemn adjuration used by all nations, quotes Aeneas swearing by sun and earth and rivers, and finds in such appeals the origin and use of oaths.

debates.question: Who or what are the witnesses summoned?

sides.position: heaven and earth personified, though inanimate
the intelligent creatures in them, angels and men, by metonymy
holders: an older exposition, rejected by Calvin

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph — that a warning delivered before the whole visible creation is harder to forget than a private one, and that Moses makes the sky and the ground parties to the transaction — is my expansion of Calvin's bare statement that the threat is put this way so that it may affect them more deeply.

27.pericope_label: Scattered among the nations, and serving the gods of wood and stone

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch refuse to limit the threat to the Assyrian period, extending it to the dispersion under Rome, and read the coming idolatry as a law of decline — image-worship leading to ever coarser forms; Ellicott takes the service as political bondage, with Rashi, and notes that a nation's gods were held to share its captivity.

Clarke reflects on the ten tribes, now indistinguishable from the idolaters among whom they dwell though God can gather them; Wesley states the principle — the very thing that was their choice becomes their punishment.

Gill identifies the scattering with the two captivities, takes the idolatry literally, but records the Targums' alternative that it means serving the peoples who serve idols, since captivity in fact cured Israel of idolatry.

debates.question: In what sense would the exiles 'serve gods of wood and stone'?

sides.position: literally, being enticed or compelled into idolatry
politically, being in bondage to the nations whose gods they were
holders: Onkelos and Jonathan (as reported by Gill)

themes: gods that neither hear nor smell

schools.summary: Gill has them seeking by prayer and confession out of the uttermost parts of the earth; Calvin explains that the promise anticipates despair, since the wretched cannot submit to God, and then guards it — 'all the heart' means an upright heart against a feigned one, though our known inability need not induce listlessness.
Clarke reads it as an open door for a backsliding people; Wesley says there is no part of the earth with a gulf fixed between it and heaven.
Keil and Delitzsch compare the prodigal son, and make the finding conditional on seeking with all the heart and soul.

30.pericope_label: Turning in tribulation, and the merciful God who does not forget the covenant

schools.summary: Gill locates the tribulation in a strange land and finds God merciful in Christ, of which Moses had a comfortable view; Calvin explains the usefulness of chastisement and ranks the two grounds of hope, God's merciful nature and, more certain to a frightened people, his perpetual covenant.
Clarke asks whether these are the times spoken of and finds no evidence of the promised turning; Wesley glosses the latter days as succeeding ages.
Keil and Delitzsch close the picture of the future here, and ground the promise in the next verse — a merciful God who does not let his people go, whose verb for forsaking means to withdraw the hand.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the argument comes last — Moses wants more than fear, and appeals to unheard-of miracles of grace in order to awaken cordial love; Ellicott finds Paul using the same reasoning for Israel's restoration, that God did not take a nation out of a nation in order to abandon it.

Gill takes the summons as a call to consult the annals of former ages; Calvin explicitly rejects that construction, and holds that Moses simply asks them to examine whether anything like it had ever happened since the creation, in any region however remote.
Wesley reads 'from one side of heaven to the other' as of the earth under heaven, and the command as asking all the inhabitants of the world.

debates.question: What does 'the days that are past' send the hearer to?

sides.position: annals and chronicles of former ages
not records but the whole span since creation, examined anywhere on earth

schools.summary: Gill piles up the degrees of the unheard-of thing; Calvin grants that the Gentiles had their apparitions but says none approach this, since here are not scattered rumours or one man's dream but more than seven hundred thousand witnesses.

Clarke explains the fear behind the question — most extraordinary manifestations of God were in judgment — and sets out the three steps: an articulate voice, a supernatural fire, and no one destroyed, for he came not to destroy but to save; Wesley glosses 'and live' as not being consumed by so glorious an appearance.

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph generalises Calvin's contrast between individual liars and 700,000 witnesses into a rule about why a national theophany can be appealed to as evidence; the logic is his, the statement of it as a principle running through the whole sermon is mine.

schools.summary: Gill says God had not merely assayed this but done it, and no parallel could be produced; Calvin notes that the verse covers the whole deliverance and not only the giving of the law, and describes Israel as an obscure part of a famous nation, rescued from its bowels.

Clarke lists what made the exodus improbable and then works through the seven means term by term, distinguishing the finger, the hand, the arm and the arm stretched out as ascending degrees of divine power; Wesley takes 'temptations' as the general title, the rest explaining it, since all were trials to Egyptian and Israelite alike.

themes: a nation taken from a nation

35.pericope_label: Shown these things to know that the LORD is God, and no other

schools.summary: Gill keeps the reference to what God did in Egypt and offers two readings of the heavenly voice, thunder or the voice at Sinai; Calvin argues from proven divinity to sole divinity, since dominion cannot be withdrawn from God and resides in one subject, and answers how the voice can be both from heaven and out of the fire.

Keil and Delitzsch place the speaking chiefly from heaven and out of the fire on Sinai, and against Schultz prefer Knobel's sense of the verb — not instruction in truth and sovereignty but taking the people under holy discipline.

debates.question: What does it mean that God spoke 'to instruct thee'?

sides.position: to instruct them concerning his truth and sovereignty
holders: Schultz (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: to take them under holy discipline, inspiring a salutary fear

themes: a voice from heaven out of the fire

37.pericope_label: Because he loved thy fathers: election, exodus and dispossession

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reject both Schultz's dependent clause and Knobel's protasis-and-apodosis as forced, taking the verses as an independent thought and the sum of the whole address; Ellicott notes that Deuteronomy always states the reason for the choice so as to enforce sovereignty and exclude merit.

Gill distinguishes the remote fathers from the generation that fell in the wilderness; Calvin allows the sentence two constructions, insists that 'love' here excludes all worthiness in the beloved, and answers the objection about eternal election by the gratuitous adoption of Abraham.

debates.question: How is the sentence to be construed?

sides.position: as dependent on what precedes
holders: Schultz (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: as protasis to the following verses
holders: Knobel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: as an independent thought, the sum of the address

39.pericope_label: Know and consider, and keep his statutes

schools.summary: Ellicott sharpens 'consider' by its use for reckoning and imputing, and turns 'there is none else' into an argument — if each nation had its deity, how does Jehovah control them all, and if you leave him there is no one else to serve; Keil and Delitzsch attach the promise of long life in the land.

Gill separates confessing with the mouth from laying up in the heart, and grounds obedience in obligation and in God's right to command; Calvin says the plainness of the evidence leaves no excuse, and has Moses confess himself only the minister of what he received.
Henry draws out both halves of the geography, notes that the heathen deities never claimed universal monarchy, and explains why consideration is commanded and not merely knowledge.

41.pericope_label: Three cities of refuge east of Jordan

schools.summary: Gill dates the act to the conquest of the two Amorite kingdoms, records Jarchi's view that the cities did not operate until the three in Canaan were set apart, and limits the refuge to the man who killed unawares; Calvin draws the lesson that a command we cannot yet fulfil entirely is no excuse for idleness.
Keil and Delitzsch explain why the notice stands here — the cities consecrated the land east of Jordan, confirmed the conquest, and set the people an example of punctual obedience.
Henry names the three by their tribes and says Moses did what he could while still with them, to give the settled rulers an example.
Clarke refers the law back to Numbers 35, reports that the cities' names have been read as attributes of the Redeemer, and conjectures that the last nine verses were added by Joshua or Ezra.

outliers.note: supposes the last nine verses of the chapter to have been added by either Joshua or Ezra.

themes: obedience as far as circumstances allow

44.pericope_label: The heading to the second address

schools.summary: Gill, with Jarchi, refers the heading forward to the ten commandments of the next chapter rather than back to the cities of refuge, and dates the material twice — Sinai in the third month, Moab near forty years later; Calvin explains that the law was published anew at the threshold of the land to dispose them to obedience, and insists nothing was added to the original summary.
Keil and Delitzsch take the two verses as a heading and a fuller description by leading features, and read 'after they came forth out of Egypt' as during the march rather than after its end.
Henry describes the transition as another sermon, probably the next sabbath, and sets the law before them as the rule to work by and the glass in which to see their natural face.
Wesley calls the verse a preface to what the next chapter expresses more punctually.

themes: the law as rule and glass

46.pericope_label: Where the address was given: the valley over against Beth-peor

schools.summary: Henry finds meaning in the two halves of the description: an idol-temple of the Moabites opposite, and their own new conquest under their feet, so that the triumph itself argued for obedience.

Gill walks the boundaries — Aroer on the Arnon, Mount Sion, the plain east of Jordan to the salt sea, under the springs of Pisgah — and notes the two Amorite kingdoms divided among two tribes and a half.

themes: preached within sight of a shrine
